Mr. Subroto Chowdhury with Ms Sonia Parvin and Ms. Bithi Roy, Advocates ------ For the petitioners. 
Mr. Probir Neogi with Mr. Zakir Hossain Ripon, Advocates ------- For the opposite parties.
parties:
MILON CHANDRA BANIK @ DHAR AND ANOTHER
Vs.
SREE SHUVASH CHANDRA DHAR AND OTHERS
full_judgment:
Khizir Ahmed Choudhury, J: The instant rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-7 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order No.11 dated 13.03.2016 passed by learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 450 of 2014 rejecting the application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedures should not be set aside.

2. Opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted other suit No. 450 of 2014 in the 1st Court of Joint district Judge, Chittagong praying for declaration of title; right to use the pond in the suit land jointly; judgment and decree passed by learned Additional Assistant Judge, Chittagong in Other Title Suit No. 41 of 1992 will not create any obstruction in the peaceful possession of the plaintiff and the defendants are not entitled to take any step by virtue of execution case No.01 of 2014 pending in the Court of Assistant Judge, 1st Additional Court, Chittagong and other reliefs.

3. The case of the plaintiff in brief is that suit property originally belonged to 2 brothers namely Ananta Mohan and Kashi Mohan whose name record of right is prepared. Ananta Mohan had no issue and Kashi Mohan died leaving behind his son Porikkhit Banik and as such the Schedule property devolved to Porikkhit Banik and he had been enjoying the property as rightful owner and possessor for a considerable period of time and his name also appeared in the P.S. Khatian No.341/1, 5878/2 and Khatian No. 341/2 as well as B.S. Khatian No. 2978. Suit land consists of house, pond and Viti type. Due to financial stringency Porikkhit Banik relinquished his right title and interest over the suit property to opposite party No.1 vide registered deed No.1655 dated 24.08.1997 who has been enjoying and possessing the suit property without any let or hindrance. On 27.06.2014 the defendant along with some others tried to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land on the pretext of a decree in respect of the suit land in a suit for specific performance of contract. To avoid untoward incidence the plaintiff filed a case under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and subsequently in order to remove the cloud constrained to file the instant suit.

4. The defendants entered appearance and by filing an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure prayed for rejection of the plaint contending that the suit property originally belonged to Mohendra Lal Dey and on his death it devolved upon his three sons Kali Shankar Dey, Hari Shankar Dey and Narayan Chandra Dey. Petitioner's father instituted Other Class Suit No. 45 of 1990 before the Subordinate Judge, Chittagong, having renumbered as Other Class Suit No.41 of 1992 having transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, first Additional Court, Chittagong, seeking specific performance of contract contending that the owners proposed to sell the suit property to the father of the petitioners and accordingly entered into a agreement on 07.12.1989 fixing Tk.60,000/- as consideration money out of which Tk.35,000/- was paid as baina money and it was stipulated that after obtaining requisite permission from Income Tax authority and observing other formalities the owners will execute and register deed of sale on receiving Tk.35,000/-. Father of the petitioner after complying terms and condition and observing formalities demanded execution and registration of deed of sale on the basis of oral contract but the owner of the property declined to execute and register deed of sale. Petitioners' father demanded on several occasions for execution and registration of the Kabala and lastly on 18.03.1990 he approached the predecessor of the defendant to execute and register deed of sale and ultimately constrained to file the suit which was decreed in favour of the predecessor of the petitioners on 31.08.1992 against which the defendants of that suit preferred Other Appeal No.521 of 1992 which was allowed whereby Judgment and Decree passed by the trial Court was set aside, against which the petitioners father filed Civil Revision No. 4756 of 1995 before the High Court Division and after hearing rule was made absolute which was challenged before the Appellate Division in Civil Petition For Leave To appeal No.81 of 2011 by the predecessor of the defendants and the Appellate Division also upheld the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division which was again challenged by the predecessor of the defendants by filing Civil review petition before the Appellate division which was also dismissed. The predecessor of defendant No.10 and 11 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.98 of 1992 before the senior assistant Judge, 5th Court, Chittagong impleading the predecessor of present petitioner as defendant, praying for declaration of title and permanent injunction which was decreed in his favour on 27.04.1996.

5. The father of the defendant No.1 and 2 preferred Other Appeal No.153 of 1996 and after hearing the Appellate Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and thereafter Parikkhit Banik preferred Civil Revision No.4903 of 1999 before the High Court Division but subsequently he withdrew the said Civil Revision. The further contention of the petitioners is that, present plaintiff deposed as DW.2 in Other Suit No.41 of 1992 and knowing well about the decree obtained by the predecessor of the petitioners purchased the suit land by registered deed of sale dated 24.08.1997 being deed No. I655 and as such the suit is barred by resjudicata and also barred under clause (b) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

6. Defendant-opposite parties by filing written objection against the prayer for rejection of plaint stated that the contents of the application does not come within the purview of order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and since the statement made in the application requires to prove by evidence it cannot be resolved through application filed under order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. They further averred that the valuation as given in the plaint is reasonable and sustainable and as such the application of Order 7 Rule 11 for rejection of plaint is liable to be rejected.

7. Learned Joint District Judge by order dated 13.03.2016 rejected the application for rejection of plaint on the ground that resjudicata is a mixed question of law and facts and it can only be decided after adducing evidence at the time of peremptory hearing, and hence the instant rule.

8. Mr. Subroto Chowdhury along with Ms. Sonia Parvin and Ms. Bithi Roy appeared for the petitioners. Mr. Subroto Chowdhury learned advocate for the petitioners submits that, in a suit for specific performance of contract, the predecessor of the petitioners got decree in his favour which was upheld up to appellate division and thereby the predecessor of the present petitioners became absolute owner and possessor of the suit property, apart from this Porikkhit Banik, who is transferee of the present plaintiff filed Title Suit No.98 of 1992 seeking declaration of title and other reliefs regarding the suit land where he got decree which was reversed by the appellate court which he challenged in the high court division and ultimately he had withdrawn the civil revision and thereafter he transferred the suit land in favour of the present plaintiff and as such the suit is clearly barred by the principle of resjudicata. He also submits that since the original owners lost in the earlier proceedings, the present suit filed by the transferee of the previous owners is malafide which is filed to cause harassment to the present petitioners and as such the suit is not maintainable. Ile next submits that the present plaintiff-opposite party as DW. 2 deposed in earlier suit having filed for specific performance of contract and he had full knowledge about the decree obtained by the predecessor of the petitioners and as he purchased the property knowing fully well about the decree, the plaint is liable to be rejected as vexatious one. He next submits that in the instant matter all the facts and circumstances amply justifies that the present suit has been initiated by a person whose predecessor lost up to appellate division and he cannot get any title from persons who lost in earlier proceedings and so the present proceeding is bound to fail and as such learned Joint District committed error in not rejecting the plaint. Mr. Subroto Chowdhury further submits that Porikkhit Banik has withdrawn Civil revision No.4903 of 1999 from the High Court division without taking permission to sue afresh and as such his subsequent transferee is precluded to initiate fresh suit on the self same cause of action and as such the suit filed by the opposite party claiming purchase of the same from Porikkhit Banik cannot be proceeded with and the plaint was required to be rejected but the Joint District Judge without adverting that vital aspect of the case rejected the application simply contending the question of resjudicata is to be decided during trial.

9. Learned advocate in support of his contention referred the case of Abdul Matin Vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh 13 BLC 30, Rezaul Karim and others Vs Moulana Md. Harun-ur-Rashid and others 12 BLC 705, Syed Md. Shah Jalal Nure Alam and others Vs Salimullah Chowdhury and others 10 MLR AD 91 and also a decision reported 22 DLR in the case of Zohural haque Moral and ors Vs Abdul Karim Molla and ors 545, A.Z.M. Khalilur Rahman Vs Md. Syed Hossain and ors 25 DLR 485.

10. Per contra Mr. Probir Neogi, learned advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that in the application filed by the predecessor of the present petitioners for rejection of plaint was on the ground of being barred by resjudicata and admittedly the question of resjudicata is to be resolved by taking evidence and as such the application filed under Order 7 Rule 11 being not entertainable the court of first instance rightly rejected the application. He further submits that in considering application under order 7 Rule 11 of the C.P. Code, the statement made in the plaint is only to be relied upon, any other applications and materials are to be kept out of consideration and the trial Court rightly rejected the application relaying upon the established principles. He submits that in the plaint a clear cause of action has been delineated by the plaintiffs and as such the statement made by the defendant-petitioner in the application filed under Order 7 Rule 11 is not to be considered by the Trial Court. He further submits that the present opposite party No.1 has purchased the suit land from Porikkhit Banik who was admitted owner of the suit property and he has got every right to retain and enjoy the suit property as absolute owner and as such without establishing right title and interest by producing papers and by adducing reliable evidence, the present petitioner are not entitled to interfere in the rightful title and possession of the plaintiff. He next submits that the valuation as made in the plaint is correct and proper valuation and the defendant-petitioner failed to show any paper to the effect that the valuation is not correct and even for undervaluation, plaint should not be rejected as the valuation can be raised an updated at any point of time since the suit was pending in the Court of Joint District Judge who possess unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction for entertaining any suit. He next submits that the present opposite party No.1 is a bonafide purchaser from the owner of the suit land and he having possessed the suit land after purchase as rightful owner, his title cannot be denied by any devices. Mr. Probir Neogi in support of his contention referred the case of Chandu Lal Agarwalla and another Vs Khalilur Rahman and others 3DLR 403, Rezaul Karim and others Vs Moulana Md. Harun-ur-Rashid and others, 12 BLC 705, Sree Chandan Ranjan Sarker Vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others 18 MLR 49, Mahbubul Haque (Md) Vs Md. A Kader Munshi 52 DLR AD 49, Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das and another Vs A.K.M. Habibur. Rahman and others 13 BLD AD 217 and Razia Sultana and another Vs Mir Shahinul Islam 22 BLC 288 in support of his contention.

11. Having gone through the pleadings, relevant papers, application and supplementary affidavit it appears that the present opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No.450 of 2014 impleading the petitioner as defendants praying for declaration of title, challenging decree passed in Other Suit No.41 of 1992 and along with a prayer for permanent injunction restraining the defendants not to dispossess him from the suit land. Admittedly the plaintiffs claimed to have purchased the suit land from Porikkhit Banik, the predecessor of defendant No. 9 and 10 of the suit by a sale deed dated 24.08.1997 being sale deed No.1655. It also appears that Porikkhit Banik prior to sale of the suit land to the present opposite party No.1 instituted title Suit No.98 of 1992 before the Senior Assistant Judge, 5th Court, Chittagong praying for declaration of title confirmation of possession and permanent injunction where he got decree in his favour on 27.04.1996 and the said decree was challenged before the District Judge, Chittagong in Other Appeal No.153 of 1996 which is transferred to Joint District Judge, Commercial Court, Chittagong and after hearing the appeal was allowed by judgment and decree dated 24.10.1999 setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court. Thereafter Porikkhit Banik preferred Civil Revision No.4903 of 1999 before the High Court division and ultimately he withdrew the said Civil Revision on 11.05.2010. While allowing the withdrawal, the High Court Division set aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court as well as the Trial Court. Now it is vitally important to look into the contents of the application for withdrawing the Civil Revision. The contents of the application for withdrawal was to the effect that on perusal of the record the plaintiff-petitioner have understood that they should not have filed the suit and now on proper understanding of overall situation have decided not to proceed with the suit. The transferor of the present plaintiff did not sought any permission to refile the suit due to any formal defect or any other reasons, rather it has been mentioned in clearest terms that they should not have filed the suit and decided not to proceed with the same. Now it is to be considered in absence of any leave from the court whether a fresh suit can be instituted by the same person or his transferee claiming title in the suit since no permission was taken for instituting a fresh suit. It appears that Porikkhit Banik who filed the earlier suit has transferred the suit land in favour of the present plaintiff who after purchase again filed the suit seeking declaration of title, permanent injunction and other identical reliefs being made in the earlier suit. It is clear that the vendor of the petitioner filed title Suit No.41 of 1992. Since vendor of the present petitioners withdrew Revisional application as well as his suit, the present petitioner being successor-in-interest is not entitled to file the instant suit. For better understanding order 23 rule 1 is reproduced bellow:

"R.1 Withdrawal of suit or abandonment of part of claim (1) At any time after the institution of a suit the plaintiff may, as against all or any of the defendants, withdraw his suit or abandon part of his claim.

(2) Where the Court is satisfied-(a) that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect, or

(b) that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject-matter of a suit or part of a claim, it may, on such terms as it thinks fit, grant the plaintiff permission to withdraw from such suit or abandon such part of a claim with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of the subject-matter of such suit or such part of a claim.

(3) Where the plaintiff withdraws from a suit, or abandons part of a claim, without the permission referred to in sub-rule (2), he shall be liable for such costs as the Court may award and shall be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of such subject-matter or such part of the claim.

(4) Nothing in this rule shall be deemed to authorise the Court to permit one of several plaintiffs to withdraw without the consent of the others."

12. Since no permission is accorded for instituting fresh suit, the present suit filed by the transferee of the previous plaintiff is not maintainable.

13. In the case of Moon Garments Industries vs Janata Bank 50 DLR it is held that

"We have considered the language of Order 23, rule 1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure which clearly gives an unqualified right to a plaintiff to withdraw from suit at any time. When the plaintiff withdraws from his suit without seeking permission to sue afresh as contemplated under rule 1(2), the plaintiff is precluded from instituting any fresh suit? In respect of the subject-matter or the claim made in the suit so withdrawn"

14. Now the question arises whether in an application under Order 7 Rule 11 this fact can be examined and scrutinized in absence of any evidence to be adduced by parties at the time of peremptory hearing. So far the factual aspect is concerned nobody is denying the suits and proceeding being carried on by the parties but only legal point to be considered whether the application under Order 7 Rule 11 can be entertained and disposed of on the point of the suit being barred by resjudicata as mentioned in the application before taking the suit to the peremptory hearing. Since the parties are not disputing the papers and documents filed by them, the documents are taken to be admitted. Now the questions come whether the suit should be carried on to the peremptory hearing or can be disposed of upon the papers and documents as kept in the record. It is fairly established here that the parties indulged in various litigation in as many as courts in respect of the suit property and in all the proceedings, the present petitioners got verdict in his favour. The present plaintiff is not claiming title otherwise from Porikkhit Banik whose predecessor lost up to appellate division and after losing in the appeal, Porikkhit Bank himself has withdrawn the revisional application. In a landmark decision reported in 53 DLR AD 12 our appellate division clearly held that if ultimate result of the suit is as clear as daylight, it should not be proceeded further rather it should be buried at its inception. The facts and circumstances of that suit are quite identical with the facts and circumstances of the present suit. In that suit the predecessor of the plaintiffs by filing title suit went up to appellate division and got decree in their favour but the defendants subsequently by filing another suit tried to challenge the decree of the earlier suit and in the circumstances our appellate division clearly held that the defendant should not be allowed to proceed with the suit as their predecessor has fought up to appellate division unsuccessfully. Similar and identical scenarios have been emerged in the present suit, so apart from order 7 rule 11 of the code of Civil Produce the court can invoke inherent jurisdiction to do justice.

15. It is fairly evident that evidence is not necessary for resolution of disputes in this matter. Although by filing application under Order 7 Rule 11 code of Civil Procedure, the petitioners raised the question of resjudicata but in fact this particular matter clearly comes within the ambit of inherent power of the Court which can take a decision in an appropriate case since the case in hand is quite identical with the facts and circumstances of the reported decisions of 53 DLR AD 12. The facts and circumstance and factual matrix as mentioned in the application clearly made out a case for exercising inherent power.

16. Mere mentioning wrong provision in the application does not invalidate any application or order where actually source of power exists, so it is a fit case for exercising inherent power of the Court and this court the suit as filed by the opposite party No.1 should not be proceeded with. Apart from this in the case of Md. Shahjahan Siraj Vs Md. Rafique Quoraishi and others 2 ALR AD 202 our appellate division held that plaint can be rejected on the ground of resjudicata and the Court is quite to consider resjudicata in an application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Relevant paragraph of the said decision is here under,

"Having gone through the plaints of both the suits, we are of the view that the plaints of both the suits were rightly rejected by the learned Additional District Judge but that should have been done by resorting to the provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil procedure. Therefore, the plaints of both the suits shall be deemed to have been rejected under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the materials on record justify to do so."

<u>17. The principles enunciated in the decision of 22 BLC 288, 18 MLR 49 are that the Court cannot travel beyond the averments made in the plaint and cannot take into consideration regarding maintainability of the suit but by this time it is fairly settled that in an appropriate case Court can reject plaint by invoking inherent power under section 151 of the code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case inherent power of the Court has been invoked given the facts and circumstances of the case and as such the referred decision is distinguishable here. The decision referred in 13 BLD AD 217, 12 BLC 705, 3 DLR 403, 52 DLR AD 49 are regarding the principals of resjudicata wherein it has been held that resjudicata is mixed question of law and fact and such plea is to be considered upon taking evidence but meanwhile it is propounded in the decision referred in 2 ALR AD 203 as referred above, that in an appropriate case the Court can reject the plaint on the question of resjudicata by invoking inherent power of the Court and the instant case being appropriate one for invoking such power given the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the decision as referred above is not applicable here as the case clearly came within the perimeter of the principals as enunciated in the decision of 2 ALR AD 203 and 53 BLR AD 12.</u>

18. Another striking feature is that the present plaintiff deposed as DW.2 in earlier proceeding whereby the predecessor of the present opposite party got decree in their favour in a suit for specific performance of contract, so he cannot be termed a person who is unaware about the litigation and outcome of the suits. Apart from this Porikkhit Banik transferred the suit land in favour of the present plaintiff although Porikkhit Banik by filing title suit seeking declaration of title lost in that suit, so it is clearly established that a clever design and many waver has been Exercised by Porikkhit Banik and present plaintiff regarding suit land for depriving the lawful owner of the suit land. The plaintiff also can't be termed as bonafide purchaser.

19. Above factual scenarios clearly establish case in favour of the petitioners. The application filed by the plaintiff for rejection of plaint merits consideration and accordingly the rule is made absolute.

20. The plaint of title Suit No.450 of 2014 pending in the court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong is rejected. The parties will bear their respective cost.

21. Communicate the order.

End.
